answer: Explain why Acts is best understood as 'volume two' of Luke's writing. What does this teach about the ongoing ministry of the risen Christ?
Why did Jesus command the disciples to wait before going on mission? What does this teach about Spirit-empowered ministry today?
Describe the three signs of Pentecost (wind, fire, tongues). What is the Old Testament background for each?
How is Pentecost the reversal of Babel? What does this say about God's plan for all nations?
Outline Peter's Pentecost sermon (Acts 2:14–41). What is the structure and what is the central claim?
The early church in Acts 2:42 had four marks: doctrine, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayers. Which of these does the modern church most often neglect, and why?
Explain Acts 1:8 as the structural outline of the entire book of Acts.
The Hebrides Revival was born in the persistent prayer of two elderly women. What does this teach about the kind of prayer God answers with revival?
What is your personal 'Jerusalem,' your 'Judea and Samaria,' and your 'end of the earth'? Be specific.
How does Acts 2:39 ('the promise is to you... to all who are afar off') apply directly to your life and ministry today?
Explain why Peter immediately deflected glory from himself after the healing of the lame man (Acts 3:12). Why does this deflection matter for ministry today?
Discuss the exclusivity claim of Acts 4:12 ('there is no other name'). How should this shape Christian witness in a pluralistic culture?
The believers prayed for boldness, not safety, after their first arrest (Acts 4:29). What does this priority teach us about prayer in persecution?
Why did God deal so severely with Ananias and Sapphira? What does this teach about hypocrisy in the church?
Explain the principle 'we ought to obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). Give a concrete example of how this might apply to a believer today.
What was wise about Gamaliel's counsel (Acts 5:34–39)? Was he himself a believer? What does his caution teach about discernment?
Discuss the appointment of the Seven (Acts 6:1–7) as a model for delegation and church leadership.
The story of Mitsuo Fuchida and Jacob DeShazer illustrates Gamaliel's warning about 'fighting against God.' Explain how the story functions as an Acts illustration.
Internal threats (Ananias) versus external threats (Sanhedrin) — which is more dangerous to a healthy church and why?
Synthesize the lessons of Acts 3–6:7 for contemporary church leaders facing both opposition and internal challenges.
Stephen had been recruited as a deacon to oversee food distribution. What does his subsequent ministry of preaching and martyrdom teach about how God uses people who simply make themselves available?
Summarize the structure of Stephen's defense in Acts 7. Why did he take his accusers all the way back to Abraham instead of answering the charges directly?
Discuss the theological significance of Stephen seeing the Son of Man standing (rather than seated) at the right hand of God (Acts 7:56).
Stephen's two prayers as he died mirror two of Christ's sayings from the cross. Identify them and discuss the meaning of the parallel.
Explain the wordplay in Acts 8:4 between 'scattered' and the Greek verb speiro ('sow'). What does this teach about persecution and gospel advance?
Why did Peter rebuke Simon the sorcerer so severely? What modern parallels exist for the sin of simony in the church today?
Trace the providence in the meeting of Philip and the Ethiopian eunuch. What elements of the story show God's sovereign orchestration of evangelism?
The Ethiopian eunuch was reading Isaiah 53. Discuss why this is the natural Old Testament passage to launch a New Testament gospel presentation.
Discuss how the Glenn Chambers 'WHY?' letter illustrates the church's question at the death of Stephen. How does Acts 8:1 begin to answer that question?
Synthesize Acts 6:8–8:40 as the launching of Acts 1:8 part two: the move from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria, and the first contact with 'the end of the earth.'

Saul thought he was serving God when he was actually fighting against God. How does this connect with Gamaliel's warning in Acts 5:39, and what does it teach about religious sincerity that is misdirected?
Discuss the significance of Christ saying 'why are you persecuting Me' rather than 'why are you persecuting My church.' What does this tell us about union with Christ?
Why is Ananias of Damascus one of the bravest men in the New Testament? What did obedience cost him, and what did it gain the church?
Christ told Ananias upfront that Saul was a 'chosen vessel' who would 'suffer many things' for His name. How should this reality of preordained suffering shape our understanding of calling?
Discuss the significance of Ananias's first words: 'Brother Saul.' What does this teach about Christian fellowship and reconciliation?
The roles of Ananias of Damascus and Barnabas in Saul's early discipleship are often overlooked. What pastoral lessons emerge from how each man received the new convert?
The persecutor became the persecuted within weeks of his conversion. What does this teach about the costs of identifying with Christ?
Why is Barnabas, more than the apostles, the unsung hero of Saul's reception in Jerusalem? Discuss the role of 'the church's Barnabases' in modern congregational life.
Acts 9:31 reports that with Saul's conversion the churches finally had peace. Discuss this irony and what it teaches about the Lord's sovereignty over persecution.

Synthesize the message of Acts 9:1–31 for a modern congregation: who are the Sauls in our streets, who are the Ananiases and Barnabases who must receive them, and what is the Lord still doing on the road to Damascus?
Discuss the symbolic significance of Peter lodging at the home of Simon the tanner before his vision in Joppa. How does Luke set up the Cornelius episode through such small details?
Explain Peter's rooftop vision (Acts 10:9-16). Why was the vision repeated three times, and why does Peter not realize at first that it is about people rather than food?
The phrase 'God shows no partiality' (Acts 10:34) is foundational to Christian missions. How does this principle reshape how the church views ethnicity and nationality?
Discuss Peter's defense of his ministry to Cornelius before the Jerusalem church (Acts 11:1-18). What does the Jerusalem church's response teach about gospel humility?
Acts 11:21 says 'the hand of the Lord was with them.' Discuss the three-fold pattern that follows when the hand of the Lord moves: conversions, commissions, and celebrations.

The Welsh Revival of 1904-05 began with a timid girl, Flory Evans, saying 'I love the Lord Jesus with all my heart.' Discuss the parallel between this story and Antioch and what it teaches about how revival begins.
The disciples were first called 'Christians' at Antioch. Discuss the original derisive sense of the term and what it means for believers today to bear the label.
The death of James (Acts 12:2) and the deliverance of Peter (Acts 12:7-11) happen in the same chapter. What does the contrast teach about the providence of God in suffering and rescue?
The story of Rhoda forgetting to open the gate (Acts 12:13-16) is a humorous moment in Acts. What gentle pastoral lesson does Luke embed in the scene?
Acts 12:23-24 places Herod's death and the gospel's growth in immediate sequence. Discuss how this contrast functions as a theological summary of the entire chapter.
Discuss the multi-ethnic composition of the Antioch leadership team in Acts 13:1. What does this teach about church leadership and gospel reach?
Why are both vertical and horizontal confirmation necessary in a missionary call (Acts 13:2-4)? Discuss the dangers of having only one without the other.
Discuss the significance of the shift from 'Barnabas and Saul' to 'Paul and his party' in Acts 13:13. What does this teach about mentoring and leadership transition?
Trace the long-arc story of John Mark from Acts 13:13 (defection) to 2 Timothy 4:11 (Paul's request for him). What does this teach about restoring those who have failed?
Discuss the structure of Paul's Pisidian Antioch sermon (Acts 13:16-41) and its theological climax in verses 38-39. How is justification by faith preached?
Acts 13:48 says 'as many as had been appointed to eternal life believed.' Discuss this verse's significance for the doctrine of election in the book of Acts.
Discuss the volatility of the Lystran crowd: garlands one hour, stones the next (Acts 14:11-19). What does this teach about the unreliability of crowd-based ministry?
Discuss Peter's argument at the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:7-11), particularly his identification of the Mosaic law as 'a yoke neither our fathers nor we were able to bear.'
Why is James's verdict at the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:13-21) particularly significant given his reputation as the most Torah-observant figure in the Jerusalem church?
Synthesize the message of Acts 12:25–16:5: how does the Lord turn opposition (Bar-Jesus, the Lystran mob, the Judaizers, the Paul-Barnabas split) into multiplied gospel advance?
Discuss the closed doors of Acts 16:6-7. Why does the Spirit sometimes forbid faithful workers, and what does the Macedonian vision teach about how God redirects His servants?
In Acts 16:14, what does Luke emphasize by saying that 'the Lord opened her heart' to heed Paul's message, and how should this verse inform a theology of conversion?
Why did Paul refuse to accept the testimony of the Philippian slave girl even though her words were factually true (Acts 16:16-18)? What does this teach about discernment?
The Itzhak Perlman story (a violinist playing a concerto on three strings after one snapped) is offered as a parallel to Paul and Silas singing in the Philippian jail. Explain the connection.
Discuss the Berean response to Paul (Acts 17:11) as a model for how local churches should evaluate teaching. What dangers exist in being either too credulous or too cynical?
Paul's Mars Hill sermon (Acts 17:22-31) starts with the Athenian altar 'To the Unknown God.' Discuss this approach as a model for engaging non-Christian cultures with the gospel.
The Athenian audience responded in three ways: mocking, delaying, and believing. Discuss why 'we will hear you again' (Acts 17:32) is described as the most dangerous response.
Discuss Paul's tentmaking partnership with Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth as a model of bivocational ministry. What does this teach about pastoral compensation and burden-bearing?
Acts 18:9-10: 'I have many people in this city.' Discuss how this verse should encourage discouraged pastors and missionaries today.
Synthesize the second missionary journey (Acts 16:6–18:22) as the gospel's first sustained engagement with European culture. What strategic lessons emerge for missions today?
Discuss Aquila and Priscilla's correction of Apollos in private (Acts 18:26) as a model for how to handle a gifted but theologically incomplete teacher today.
The 12 Ephesian disciples had repented and been baptized but had not heard the gospel. What does this teach about religious practice without Christ?
Discuss the principle that 'there are two ways' (the Didache, Wayne's framework). What dangers exist in walking a road that is close to the gospel road but not the gospel road?
Acts 19:10 says all who dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord during Paul's two years in Tyrannus's school. What does this teach about the strategy of sustained daily teaching?
The demon's reply 'Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?' (Acts 19:15) is one of the most chilling sentences in Acts. What does it teach about borrowed Christian vocabulary?
The Ephesian believers burned their magic books at great financial cost (Acts 19:19). Discuss what 'fifty thousand pieces of silver' represents and what modern equivalents might exist.
Demetrius the silversmith argued that Paul's gospel threatened both their trade and the goddess Diana. Discuss the relationship between the gospel and economic interests in Acts 19 and today.
The Eutychus episode (Acts 20:7-12) is told with quiet humor by Luke. What pastoral lessons emerge from this story about preaching length and the Lord's grace?
Discuss Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus (Acts 20:17-38). What is meant by 'the whole counsel of God' and 'warning everyone night and day with tears'?

Synthesize Paul's response to Agabus's prophecy and the church's pleas (Acts 21:13-14): 'I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem.' What does this model about courage and submission to God's will?
James proposed Paul demonstrate his Jewish faithfulness by paying for four men's Nazirite sacrifices. Discuss the wisdom and risks of this advice (Acts 21:17-26).
Discuss the parallels between Paul's arrest in Jerusalem and Christ's last hours. Why does Luke embed these parallels into the narrative of Acts 21-26?
Paul's Hebrew (Aramaic) speech on the barracks stairs (Acts 22) is a model of contextualized witness. Discuss how he identifies with his hearers before challenging them.
The crowd listened to Paul until he mentioned the Gentiles. Discuss why ethnic and religious pride often shipwrecks the gospel and how to navigate it.
Discuss Paul's strategic use of his Roman citizenship (Acts 22:25). When should Christians invoke legal protections, and when should they not?
Paul rebuked the high priest Ananias as a 'whitewashed wall' but immediately corrected himself when told who he was (Acts 23:3-5). What does this teach about pastoral self-correction?
Discuss Paul's strategic declaration before the Sanhedrin: 'I am a Pharisee... judged for the resurrection' (Acts 23:6). Was this manipulation, witness, or both?
Acts 23:11: 'Be of good cheer, Paul; as you have testified for Me in Jerusalem, so you must bear witness at Rome.' Discuss this verse as a theological summary of providence in suffering.
The forty-man oath plot was foiled by Paul's unnamed nephew (Acts 23:16). Discuss what this story teaches about the Lord's use of the overlooked and the young.
Synthesize Acts 21:17–23:35 as the beginning of Paul's journey to Rome. How does the Lord weave hostile politics, mob violence, and bureaucratic protection into one missionary itinerary?
Discuss the rhetorical strategy of Tertullus's flattery of Felix (Acts 24:2-4) compared to Paul's measured defense (Acts 24:10-21). What does this teach about courtroom integrity?
Felix said, 'Go away for now; when I have a convenient time I will call for you' (Acts 24:25). Discuss why procrastination is one of the most dangerous responses to gospel preaching.
Discuss Paul's strategic use of his right to appeal to Caesar (Acts 25:11). How does this fit with the Lord's earlier promise that Paul would witness in Rome?
Agrippa II's reply, 'You almost persuade me to become a Christian' (Acts 26:28), is one of the saddest sentences in the New Testament. Discuss the danger of being 'almost' converted.
Paul's reply to Agrippa included 'except for these chains' (Acts 26:29). Discuss what this teaches about the freedom of the imprisoned Christian and the bondage of the unconverted king.
The first principle for surviving a storm is 'know in whom to believe.' Using Acts 27:25 ('I believe God'), discuss the difference between faith in an outcome and faith in a Person.
The second principle for surviving a storm is 'know when to wait.' Discuss why waiting is the hardest discipline in the Christian life.
The third principle for surviving a storm is 'know when to walk away' (Acts 27:31). Discuss how this principle applies to grief, dead relationships, and past failures.
Acts 28:15 records that the Roman believers walked out to meet Paul on the Appian Way and 'Paul thanked God and took courage.' Discuss the importance of small welcomes in pastoral ministry.

Acts 28:31 ends Luke's narrative mid-story, with Paul still 'preaching… teaching… no one forbidding him.' Discuss why the book of Acts has no formal ending and what this teaches about the ongoing mission.
Discuss why the Holy Spirit deliberately left the book of Acts without a formal ending and what theological weight this carries for the ongoing church.

Trace the gospel's progression through ethnic and social categories in Acts (Jerusalem Jews → Hellenists → Samaritans → Ethiopian → Saul → Cornelius → Antioch Gentiles → philosophers → Caesar's household). What does this teach us?
Discuss Acts 4:13 ('they had been with Jesus') as the only credential that ultimately matters in ministry. How does this challenge modern theological education?
Acts shows the gospel traveling through ordinary believers (Stephen, Philip, Aquila and Priscilla, unnamed refugees, the unnamed nephew). Discuss the implications for lay ministry today.
The gospel costs something throughout Acts. Discuss specific costs (martyrdoms, beatings, financial losses) and contrast with health-and-wealth theology.
Discuss how the Lord turned every opposing force (Sanhedrin, Herod, Demetrius, the storm, the chain) into part of the gospel's itinerary. What does this teach about providence?
Discuss the danger of being 'almost' a Christian (Agrippa) or postponing for a 'convenient time' (Felix). How should this shape gospel urgency?
Reflect personally on which character or scene in Acts has shaped you most this term, and why.
Wayne's three final charges (Acts 1:8 witness; Acts 4:13 with Jesus; Acts 28:31 with all confidence) form a closing triad. Apply each to your own ministry calling.
Write the opening paragraph of YOUR Acts 29 — the next chapter of the unfinished book. What do you sense the Lord asking you to write next?
Explain what John 1:1 teaches about who the Word is.
What does John 1:3 teach about the Word and creation, and why does it matter?
Explain John 1:14, "the Word became flesh," and the meaning of "dwelt among us."
Describe John the Baptist as a witness, and what makes a true witness.
Explain the contrast in John 1:11–12 between His own rejecting Him and those who received Him.
What does it mean that those who received Him were "born... of God" (John 1:13)?
Explain John 1:18, that the Son has "declared" the Father.
Why does John begin his Gospel in eternity rather than at Bethlehem?
Describe the divine-and-human pattern ("as a man... but as God...") in the person of Christ.
What is the purpose of the whole Gospel of John, and how does the Prologue serve it?
Explain what Jesus meant by being "born again" / "born from above" (John 3:3), and why it is necessary.
What did Nicodemus misunderstand, and what does this teach about the natural mind and spiritual things?
Explain the wind illustration (John 3:8) and what it teaches about the Spirit's work in the new birth.
"Flesh gives birth to flesh, but the Spirit to spirit" (John 3:6). Explain the two births.
Who brings about the new birth, and what does that say about human ability?
Why is the new birth essential and not optional (John 3:5, 7)?
Explain the bronze serpent (John 3:14–15) and how it pictures the cross.
Explain John 3:16 and the meaning of the word "whoever."
What does John 3:17–19 teach about Christ coming to save rather than condemn, and about light and darkness?
What is the radical transformation of the new birth, becoming a "new creature"?
Explain what Jesus meant by "living water" (John 4:10–14) and how it differs from well water.
Describe the barriers Jesus crossed to reach the Samaritan woman, and what this shows.
Explain "God is Spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth" (John 4:23–24).
How did Jesus reveal Himself as Messiah here, and why is it striking that He did so to this woman?
Describe how the Samaritan woman became the town's first evangelist ("come and see").
Explain the "Divine Partnership" taught from John 4:34–38 and Philippians 2:13.
Explain "the fields are already white for harvest" (John 4:35).
Why is the contrast between the woman and the silent disciples significant?
Describe the different kinds of evangelists and the truth they teach about the church.
What does it mean that salvation and purpose are found only in Christ, the Living Water?
Why is the feeding of the five thousand unique among the miracles, and how does it carry us back to Moses in the wilderness?
Describe how Philip and Andrew each responded to the hungry crowd, and why John notes that Jesus already knew what He would do.
What moved Jesus to feed the crowd, and what does the lesson say about the supposed difference between the God of the Old Testament and Jesus?
Tell the story of Mary Reed and explain what it illustrates about the compassion of the Bread of Life.
What do the twelve baskets of fragments teach, and how do the widow of Zarephath and Dr. Cook's own testimony reinforce that lesson?
Why did Jesus withdraw when the crowd wanted to make Him king by force, and what does 'The Creator is no man's debtor' warn against?
Describe Jesus walking on the sea. What is the significance of His words 'It is I; do not be afraid,' and what happened when the disciples received Him into the boat?
Why did the crowd seek Jesus the next day, and how did He answer their appeal to Moses and the manna?
What is the real hunger of our age, what do people try to fill it with, and what did Augustine finally conclude?
What was the 'hard saying' of John 6:51, how did the crowd and Peter respond, and what obligation does the lesson draw for us?
Explain "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12) and what it means to follow Him.
Explain how "light dispels the darkness" (John 1:5; 3:19–20).
How is Jesus the visible image of the invisible God, and how does He relate to the law?
Explain "before Abraham was, I AM" (John 8:58) and why the leaders reacted as they did.
Explain how Jesus is fully God and fully man, drawing on John 8.
Explain the disciples' "who sinned?" question and Jesus' answer about the man's blindness (John 9:1–3).
Describe the healing of the man born blind (clay, Siloam) as a sign of the Light.
Trace the man's progressive confession of who Jesus is.
Explain "true sight is a matter of the heart, not the eyes" and the Pharisees' blindness (John 9:39–41).
What do the seven "I AM" sayings in John reveal about who Jesus is?
Explain how John's Gospel functions as a courtroom and why the witnesses matter (John 20:31).
Describe the Bethesda healing and why it provoked the charge against Jesus.
Explain the witness of the Father and of Jesus' works (John 5:36-37).
Explain the witness of the Scriptures and of Moses (John 5:39, 46).
Explain the witness of the Holy Spirit (Cook's added witness for today).
Why is Jesus' own testimony true even when He testifies of Himself (John 8:14-18)?
Describe how the Samaritan woman and the man born blind each became a witness to Christ.
Describe how the nobleman and Mary Magdalene each became a witness to Christ.
Explain the tragedy of John 5:40 and what it reveals about unbelief.
Explain the verdict of John 20:31 and the believer's own call to be a witness.
Explain our condition as straying sheep (Isaiah 53:6) and our need of a shepherd.
Explain "I am the door" and how the hillside shepherd literally became the door (10:7-9).
Contrast the thief with the abundant life Jesus gives (John 10:10).
Explain why Jesus is the only door of access to God.
Explain that the Good Shepherd knows His sheep by name (John 10:3, 14).
Explain how the sheep come to know the Shepherd's voice (John 10:4, 27).
Contrast the good shepherd and the hireling (John 10:11-13).
Explain that the Good Shepherd lays down His life, and what "good" means here (10:11, 18).
Explain the security of the sheep in Christ's hand (John 10:27-30).
Explain the meaning of the two men reciting Psalm 23 (knowing the Shepherd).
Summarize the four movements of John 11 — the tragedy, trial, and tears of death, and the triumph over death.
Explain why Cook says death is a tragedy even for believers.
Why did Jesus delay, and what does "this sickness is for the glory of God" mean (John 11:4)?
Explain how God uses trials to grow our faith (Paul's thorn; Sangster's son).
Explain the meaning of "Jesus wept" (John 11:35).
Explain the meaning of "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25-26).
Explain the significance of "Lazarus, come forth" (John 11:43).
Explain "Loose him, and let him go" and the part the church plays (John 11:44).
How does this sign conquer the fear of death, and how did Jesus picture death (a sleep)?
Why is the raising of Lazarus the greatest of the signs, and what does "if you believe you will see the glory of God" call us to (11:40)?
Explain the request "Sir, we would see Jesus" and how it marks the hour of glory (John 12:20-23).
Explain the grain of wheat and how Jesus' glory comes through death (John 12:24).
Explain how the grain-of-wheat principle applies to the disciple (John 12:25-26).
Explain the voice from heaven and what it revealed (John 12:27-30).
Explain what "glory" means and how Jesus reveals it (John 1:14).
Describe the foot-washing and what it shows about greatness (John 13:4-5).
Explain God's measure of greatness versus the world's.
Explain "you also ought to wash one another's feet" and how we do it today (John 13:14-15).
Explain the new commandment and the sign it gives to the world (John 13:34-35).
How does the hour of glory reveal glory through death and servanthood, and what does it call us to?
Explain how Jesus comforts His troubled disciples with the promise of the Father's house (John 14:1-3).
Explain "I am the way" and why Jesus is the only way to the Father (John 14:6).
Explain "I am the truth" and "I am the life" (John 14:6).
Explain "I am the true vine, and My Father is the vinedresser" (John 15:1).
Explain how and why the Father prunes the branches (John 15:2).
Explain what it means to "abide in Me" (John 15:4).
Explain "apart from Me you can do nothing" (John 15:5).
Explain why bearing fruit is not automatic and how it comes (John 15:4-5).
Describe the kinds of fruit the abiding believer bears (John 15:5-8; Galatians 5).
How do "the Way" and "the true Vine" fit together, and what do they call us to?
Explain why Jesus said it was to the disciples' advantage that He go away (John 16:7).
Explain the name and work of the Helper, the Spirit of truth (John 14:16-17, 26).
Explain how the Spirit testifies of Christ and convicts the world (John 15:26; 16:8-11).
Explain that the Spirit glorifies Christ, and what that means for the believer (John 16:13-14).
Explain Jesus' promise that their sorrow will turn to joy (John 16:20-22).
Explain how God reveals His plan day by day, not all at once (John 16:25-31).
Explain how John 17 shows Jesus as our great High Priest praying.
Explain Jesus' definition of eternal life and His prayer to sanctify the disciples (John 17:3, 17).
Explain that Jesus prayed for all who would believe, and the request for unity (John 17:20-23).
How do the Spirit and the High-Priestly Prayer together show that Jesus did not leave us as orphans?
Describe the betrayal and arrest, and how Jesus showed He was no helpless victim (John 18).
Explain the King's mock coronation and Pilate's "Behold the Man" (John 19:1-5).
Explain how the cross became the King's true throne (John 19:15-22).
Explain the meaning of "It is finished" (John 19:30).
Explain why John stresses that Jesus gave up His spirit (John 19:30).
Describe Mary Magdalene as the first witness of the risen Christ (John 20:1-18).
Explain Thomas's doubt and his great confession (John 20:24-29).
Explain how Jesus restored Peter by the fire (John 21:15-17).
Explain what the resurrection shows about failure and death.
Explain John's stated purpose (John 20:31) and how the whole Gospel calls for a verdict.
Why does Matthew open his Gospel with a genealogy, and what do the titles 'Son of David' and 'Son of Abraham' signify?
Discuss the women named in the genealogy and what their inclusion teaches about grace.
Explain the meaning of the two names given to the child, 'Jesus' and 'Immanuel.'
Explain the double-fulfillment of Isaiah 7:14, both in the day of Ahaz and in Jesus.
Explain Hosea 11:1 ('Out of Egypt I called My son') and how recapitulation appears in the 40 years and 40 days.
Who were the Magi, and what does their visit reveal about who Jesus is?
Contrast Herod and Jesus as two kings set side by side in Matthew 2.
Describe the three gifts of the Magi and the significance the lesson gives to each.
How does the fulfillment motif tie Matthew 1-2 together into one message?
What is the central truth about Jesus' identity that Unit 1 establishes before His ministry begins?
Who was John the Baptist, what was his message, and what prophecy did he fulfill?
Why would John not let the people rest in being 'children of Abraham,' and what is true repentance?
What is the difference between John's baptism with water and the baptism the Coming One would bring?
Why did the sinless Jesus submit to baptism, and what does 'to fulfill all righteousness' mean?
Describe what happened at the Jordan that reveals God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Explain the temptation as recapitulation — how Jesus is the true Israel and the new Adam.
Describe the three temptations and how Jesus answered each.
How does Matthew see Isaiah's prophecy of light fulfilled when Jesus begins His work in Galilee?
Why is it significant that Jesus' first preaching is the same as John's, and what does it show about the kingdom?
Describe the calling of the first disciples and what it teaches about how the King gathers His kingdom.
Describe the setting of the Sermon on the Mount and how Jesus is like a new Moses. What do the Beatitudes describe?
What does it mean to be 'poor in spirit,' and how does the unit contrast it with the Pharisee?
What is biblical meekness, and what is it NOT? Use the unit's examples.
What does it mean to hunger and thirst for righteousness, and what is promised? Use the Shackleton illustration.
How does the unit define mercy, and what does the Napoleon story teach about it?
Explain the 'pure in heart' using the window illustration, and state the promise given.
What does the unit say a peacemaker is and is not, and why are peacemakers called sons of God?
Explain what Jesus means by calling His people 'salt' and 'light,' and what He calls them to do.
Explain Matthew 5:17 and Dr. Cook's teaching on why the Law was given and how Jesus fulfilled it.
Taken as a whole, what do the Beatitudes reveal about the character of the kingdom, and whom do they portray?
How does the Sermon on the Mount move from character to practice in chapters 6-7?
What does Jesus teach about giving, praying, and fasting, and what is the key question?
Explain Jesus' teaching on treasure, the heart, and serving two masters.
How does Jesus answer anxiety in Matthew 6, and what does He command?
What does Jesus mean by 'judge not,' and how is it not a ban on all discernment?
What do 'ask, seek, knock' and the Golden Rule teach about God and about others?
Describe the two gates, the two kinds of teachers, and the two claims in Matthew 7.
Explain the parable of the two builders and how the whole sermon comes to rest on it.
Why does Jesus warn that saying 'Lord, Lord' is not enough?
What is the overall message of Matthew 6-7, and what response does it call for?
Why is the Lord's Prayer called a 'model' or 'pattern' prayer, and how are its six petitions arranged?
What does the word 'Our' teach us about prayer?
Explain the two meanings of 'Father' and what is unique about calling the Christian God 'Father.'
What does 'who art in heaven' teach, and why is it better to think of heaven's quality than its location?
Explain the petition 'Hallowed be thy name' and the examples that show what it means.
What does 'name' mean in Hebrew, and how is true reverence for God's name shown?
Explain 'Thy kingdom come' — what a kingdom is, and how the kingdom is past, present, and coming.
